task: Copyedit this finished longer fictional story, roughly 300–400 words, only if a real language or continuity problem needs repair. The brief explicitly permits an omniscient narrator, collective history, and access to private motives. Preserve the distinct episodes that show a waiting custom becoming an inheritance, rather than treating length itself as a defect. Do not force a close viewpoint, replace temporal compression with fully dramatised scenes, or add a moral. Return the story unchanged if it already works.
input:
At first the town blamed the clock. By the second winter, people had learned to gather before the hour and wait. Only the keeper knew why the tower rang a minute late: he liked the square best in the pause before the bells. He never said so. When asked, he took off his spectacles and spoke of old gears, though there was nothing wrong with them.

The baker used the interval to shake flour from her sleeves. A carrier, who was new to the town, spent it looking from his watch to the dial and back again. For a week he complained to anyone who would listen. Then he began bringing a folding stool. He set it beside the baker's basket, and she saved him the heel of the first loaf. Neither called this an improvement in the clock.

Once, the council sent a repairer. She climbed the tower, examined the clean teeth of the wheels and came down carrying the key she had been given. The keeper had asked her not to alter the setting. "It keeps time," she told the councillors. "You have chosen when to ring it." They entered a note in the ledger and did not ask her back.

Children grew into apprentices; apprentices took shops of their own. The baker's daughter inherited the oven and the carrier's stool. When the keeper could no longer manage the stairs, his successor found a pencilled instruction inside the case: leave the hand where it is. She obeyed it. She had been one of the children who waited in the square and saw no reason to make them hurry now.

The brass plate beside the tower door lost a letter, then another. Strangers occasionally asked whose name had been there. No one could answer with confidence, although everyone could explain where to stand out of the rain. The minute remained. Long after the keeper's name had faded from the brass plate, the town still kept that small appointment with silence.

A new protagonist whose close viewpoint replaces the authorised omniscient narration.

Removal of the baker, carrier, repairer, or successor episodes solely to make the story shorter.
An appended universal lesson about patience or punctuality.
